problem.paragraph: Level curves for barometric pressure (in millibars) are shown for 6:00 am on a day in November. A deep low with pressure $$972$$ mb is moving over northeast Iowa. The distance along the red line from $$K$$ (Kearney, Nebraska) to $$S$$ (Sioux City, Iowa) is $$300$$ km. Estimate the value of the directional derivative of the pressure function at Kearney in the direction of Sioux City. What are the units of the directional derivative?

image.alt: Details A contour map has been superimposed on a map of the outline of a few states. The contour map consists of concentric, almost circular loops. The innermost loop is labeled 972 and lies completely within Iowa. The second one is labeled 976 and passes through a point labeled S on the left. The next curves are labeled 980, 984, 988, 992, 996, 1000, 1004, and 1008. Parts of some curves labeled 1012, 1016, 1020, 1024 are visible on the right and some on the left. The curve labeled 1000 touches a point labeled K at the bottom left.

problem.paragraph: The contour map shows the average maximum temperature for November 2004 (in $$^{{^\circ}}C$$ ). Estimate the value of the directional derivative of this temperature function at Dubbo, New South Wales, in the direction of Sydney. What are the units?

image.alt: Details A contour map is drawn over the outline of New South Wales. The first curve labeled 30 enters from the top left, goes down and then up, goes up to the right, above Dubbo, and exits at the top left. The second curve, labeled 27, enters slightly below the Murray River, almost runs along the river, then goes up to the right, bulges toward the coast near Barrington Tops, goes up and exits to the right of 30. A small portion at the top right corner also falls under this curve. Between the exiting curve and the top right corner a small closed curve, labeled 24, is drawn. The third curve, labeled 24, enters below 27, almost runs parallel to it, bulges upward directly below Dubbo, goes down and exits just above Sydney. The next curve is labeled 21, enters at the bottom briefly and exits, enters again, bulges toward Sydney, and exits at the bottom. The last curve labeled 18, enters and exits within the previous curve, almost following the same path, running almost parallel to it.

exercises.instruction: 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, and 32 Find the maximum rate of change of $$f$$ at the given point and the direction in which it occurs.

list.item: Show that a differentiable function $$f$$ decreases most rapidly at $$\mathbf{x}$$ in the direction opposite the gradient vector, that is, in the direction of $$- \nabla f{(\mathbf{x})}$$ , and that the maximum rate of decrease is $$\left| - \nabla f\left. (\mathbf{x}) \right| \right.$$
Use the result of part (a) to find the direction in which the function $$f{({x,y})} = x^{4}y - x^{2}y^{3}$$ decreases fastest at the point $$({2, - 3})$$ . What is the rate of decrease?

problem.paragraph: Find the directions in which the directional derivative of $$f{({x,y})} = x^{2} + xy^{3}$$ at the point $$({2,1})$$ has the value $$2$$ .
Find all points at which the direction of greatest rate of change of the function $$f{({x,y})} = x^{2} + y^{2} - 2x - 4y$$ is $$\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}$$ .

solution.paragraph: All points on the line $$y = x + 1$$

problem.paragraph: Near a buoy, the depth of a lake at the point with coordinates $$({x,y})$$ is $$z = 200 + 0.02x^{2} - 0.001y^{3}$$ , where $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ are measured in meters. A fisherman in a small boat starts at the point $$({80,60})$$ and moves toward the buoy, which is located at $$({0,0})$$ . Is the water under the boat getting deeper or shallower when he departs? Explain.

The temperature $$T$$ in a metal ball is inversely proportional to the distance from the center of the ball, which we take to be the origin. The temperature at the point $$({1,2,2})$$ is $$120^{{^\circ}}$$ .

list.item: Find the rate of change of $$T$$ at $$({1,2,2})$$ in the direction toward the point $$({2,1,3})$$ .
Show that at any point in the ball the direction of greatest increase in temperature is given by a vector that points toward the origin.

problem.paragraph: Suppose you are climbing a hill whose shape is given by the equation $$z = 1000 - 0.005x^{2} - 0.01y^{2}$$ , where $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ are measured in meters, and you are standing at a point with coordinates $$({60,40,966})$$ . The positive $$x$$ -axis points east and the positive $$y$$ -axis points north.

list.item: If you walk due south, will you start to ascend or descend? At what rate?
If you walk northwest, will you start to ascend or descend? At what rate?
In which direction is the slope largest? What is the rate of ascent in that direction? At what angle above the horizontal does the path in that direction begin?

The directional derivative of $$f$$ at $$A$$ in the direction of the vector $$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$$ is $$3$$ and the directional derivative at $$A$$ in the direction of $$\overset{\rightarrow}{AC}$$ is $$26$$ . problem.paragraph: Where does the helix $$\mathbf{r}{(t)} = {\langle{\cos\pi t,\sin\pi t,t}\rangle}$$ intersect the paraboloid $$z = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ ? What is the angle of intersection between the helix and the paraboloid? (This is the angle between the tangent vector to the curve and the tangent plane to the paraboloid.)

The helix $$\mathbf{r}{(t)} = {\langle{\cos{({\pi t \slash 2})},\sin{({\pi t \slash 2})},t}\rangle}$$ intersects the sphere $$x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2} = 2$$ in two points. Find the angle of intersection at each point.

Suppose that the directional derivatives of $$f{({x,y})}$$ are known at a given point in two nonparallel directions given by unit vectors $$\mathbf{u}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ . Is it possible to find $$\nabla f$$ at this point? If so, how would you do it?

solution.paragraph: If $$\mathbf{u} = {\langle{a,b}\rangle}$$ and $$\mathbf{v} = {\langle{c,d}\rangle}$$ , then $$af_{x} + bf_{y}$$ and $$cf_{x} + df_{y}$$ are known, so we solve linear equations for $$f_{x}$$ and $$f_{y}$$ .
